articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities and Individuals, Imposes Cuba Sanctions, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations related to Iran and a designation concerning Cuba. This action is part of ongoing efforts to counter activities deemed contrary to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses (GLs) and updated its Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs). These updates aim to provide clarity and guidance to the public regarding the scope and application of the new sanctions and existing regulations.

The specific details of the designated entities and individuals, as well as the provisions of the new and amended GLs and FAQs, are available on the Treasury Department's website. These measures underscore the U.S. government's commitment to enforcing its sanctions programs against state sponsors of terrorism and human rights abusers.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation. This action indicates a recalibration of sanctions policy concerning individuals or entities previously targeted under the Venezuela sanctions program.

Designation removals typically follow a review of the circumstances that led to the initial sanction, often involving a change in behavior or status of the designated party. Such removals can signal a potential shift in diplomatic or economic engagement.

Further details regarding the specific entity or individual removed from the sanctions list are available on OFAC's recent actions page. This development will be closely watched for its implications on the broader sanctions landscape related to Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities. These actions aim to disrupt illicit financial networks and prevent the flow of funds to criminal and terrorist organizations.

These designations underscore the U.S. government's ongoing commitment to combating global illicit activities that threaten national security and international stability. The targeted individuals and entities are now subject to asset blocking and other restrictions.

The Treasury Department's announcement provides specific information on the newly designated parties and the reasons for their inclusion on the sanctions lists. Financial institutions and other regulated entities are advised to review their compliance programs to ensure adherence to these new measures.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, Designates International Criminal Court Officials, and Removes Burma-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics for apparent violations of sanctions regulations. This settlement highlights the importance of robust compliance programs for companies engaged in international trade and logistics.

In separate actions, OFAC also designated individuals associated with the International Criminal Court and issued related General Licenses. Additionally, a Burma-related designation was removed, indicating a reassessment of sanctions against certain parties connected to the region.

These diverse actions reflect OFAC's multifaceted approach to enforcing sanctions, addressing various threats, and adapting to evolving geopolitical landscapes. Further details on each action are available on the OFAC website.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License (GL). This GL authorizes certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the Russia sanctions program, providing specific exemptions for particular activities.

General Licenses are frequently used by OFAC to carve out humanitarian aid, certain financial transactions, or other activities deemed to be in the U.S. national interest, without undermining the broader sanctions regime. This new GL aims to facilitate specific, permissible engagements.

Entities and individuals involved in Russia-related transactions should carefully review the terms and conditions of this new General License to ensure compliance. The full text of the GL is available on the OFAC website.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Issues New Iran and Amended Russia General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations, further expanding the scope of sanctions targeting the Iranian regime. These designations aim to disrupt networks supporting activities deemed destabilizing to regional and international security.

In conjunction with these actions, OFAC issued a new Iran-related General License (GL) and an amended Russia-related General License. These licenses provide specific authorizations for certain transactions, offering clarity on permissible activities amidst the ongoing sanctions regimes.

The details of the newly designated entities and individuals, as well as the precise scope of the new and amended GLs, are published on the OFAC website. These measures reflect the U.S. government's continued pressure on Iran while also refining existing sanctions against Russia.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Designation Removals and Updates, Publishes Iran-Related Alert and Amended FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced several designation removals and updates, reflecting ongoing adjustments to its sanctions lists. These changes can occur due to various factors, including changes in circumstances of designated parties or policy reviews.

Additionally, OFAC published an Iran-related Alert and an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). The Alert warns foreign financial institutions that they could be targeted without advance notice for transacting with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions, as part of 'Operation Economic Outcast.'

The amended FAQ 156 removes prior language suggesting OFAC would generally contact foreign financial institutions before making a finding of sanctionable activity, emphasizing the heightened risk for those with exposure to Iranian banks.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Global Sanctions and Export Controls Blog

articles.headline: OFAC Implements New Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter terrorism activities. These actions are part of a continuous effort to disrupt the financial networks of terrorist organizations globally.

These designations impose significant restrictions on the targeted parties, including the blocking of assets and prohibitions on transactions with U.S. persons. The aim is to isolate these entities from the international financial system.

The Treasury Department's announcement provides specific details on the newly designated individuals and entities. Financial institutions are urged to review their screening processes to ensure compliance with these latest counter terrorism measures.

articles.headline: Bank of England Expected to Raise Interest Rates to 4.0% in November Amid Persistent Inflation
body: A majority of economists polled by Reuters now anticipate the Bank of England (BoE) will raise its Bank Rate to 4.0% in November, marking the first rate hike in over three years. This reversal in expectations is driven by persistently high inflation, which has remained above the BoE's 2.0% target for more than five years.

Despite the UK economy consistently outperforming expectations, inflation currently stands at 3.1% and is projected to rise to approximately double the target. Energy price increases, partly stemming from the US-Israeli war with Iran, have not yet fully translated into broader consumer price rises, but concerns remain.

While markets are fully pricing in four quarter-point rate rises by the end of next year, there is no clear majority among economists for further rate increases beyond November. Government bond yields have surged to multi-decade highs, further complicating the fiscal outlook ahead of the Chancellor's budget later this month.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes Record $750 Million Penalty on Bank of America for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a historic $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A., for widespread and egregious violations of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and its implementing regulations. This represents the largest civil money penalty in OCC history.

The OCC found that Bank of America's BSA/AML compliance program was deficient and ineffective, with systemic breakdowns in internal controls, inadequate staffing expertise, weak independent testing, and insufficient training. The bank's transaction monitoring system failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions, leading to numerous late Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs) involving billions of dollars.

Despite a December 2024 cease-and-desist order requiring the bank to address its BSA/AML deficiencies, Bank of America failed to prioritize compliance, leading to the continued processing of millions of dollars in payments in apparent violation of sanctions programs targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency / U.S. Treasury

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Penalty Against American Express for BSA/AML Program Deficiencies
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) announced a cease-and-desist order and a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank for significant deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and anti-money laundering (AML) compliance program.

The OCC determined that American Express failed to establish and maintain a BSA/AML compliance program reasonably designed to assure and monitor compliance with the BSA and its implementing regulations. Deficiencies included inadequate resources, insufficient staff expertise, systemic internal control gaps, weak independent testing, and inadequate BSA/AML training.

The bank's BSA/AML risk assessment was found to be improperly tailored, focusing on its demand deposit business rather than its more dominant credit and charge card products. This led to failures in customer due diligence, customer identification program procedures, and the timely identification and reporting of approximately $13 billion in suspected trade-based money laundering activity over the past decade.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency

body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
